What are the odds that 10 of 40 neurons fire together?

Feiyu (Ethan) Lu

Anthropic’s IPO sent me back to Dario Amodei’s Princeton physics dissertation and a 2014 paper he coauthored with Gašper Tkačik, Olivier Marre and colleagues. Forty neurons can produce more than a trillion patterns of firing and silence. The researchers had just 283,041 time windows. How do you predict a pattern you’ve barely seen? Amodei’s dissertation · Searching for Collective Behavior in a Large Network of Sensory Neurons · IPO coverage

The team showed a salamander retina the same 19-second movie 297 times while recording 160 neurons. In each 20-millisecond window, a cell got a 1 if it fired at least once and a 0 if it stayed silent. Pick 40 cells and add their ones. Call that number K. A burst of ten means exactly ten cells fired, in any combination. Original recording

What independence predicts

Imagine that each of the 40 cells fires independently with probability p. For one specific set of ten to fire while the other thirty stay silent, multiply ten factors of p and thirty of (1 − p). There are C(40, 10) ways to pick those ten, so

P(K=10)=(4010)p10(1−p)30

Real neurons have different firing rates. The paper’s independent model gives each cell its own probability, multiplies the appropriate firing and silence probabilities for each pattern, and adds up the patterns with ten active cells. It preserves every cell’s average. What it loses is the tendency of particular cells to fire together.

What a pair adds

The researchers also measured how often each pair fired in the same window. Forty cells give 40 firing rates and 780 distinct pairs. Many distributions over a trillion patterns can match those 820 numbers. Maximum entropy picks the one that leaves the greatest uncertainty about everything else. In the 0/1 notation above, it assigns each pattern s the probability

P(s)=1Zexp(∑ihisi+∑i<jJijsisj)

Read the formula as a recipe. Add hᵢ for each active cell. Add Jᵢⱼ for each pair that fired together. Exponentiate, then divide by Z, the sum of the weights of all patterns. The researchers adjust the single-cell and pair terms until the model matches the recorded rates and coincidences. The frequency of ten-cell bursts is then a prediction. Model and fitting method

Take a made-up three-neuron example. Each neuron fires in half the windows, and each pair fires together in 30%. Independence would give all eight patterns a probability of 12.5%. The maximum-entropy fit gives 20% each to 000 and 111, and 10% each to the six mixed patterns. You can check the first and third cells yourself. They fire together in 101 or 111, so their overlap is 10% + 20% = 30%.

You can recover the fitted terms from these numbers. Going from 000 to 100 halves the probability, so exp(h) = 1/2 and h = −ln 2. Going from 100 to 101 leaves the probability unchanged, so exp(h + J) = 1 and J = ln 2. The pattern 101 has two active cells and one active pair. Its weight is exp(−ln 2 − ln 2 + ln 2) = 1/2. The eight weights sum to 5, giving P(101) = 0.5/5 = 10%. How can 101 become less common even as cells 1 and 3 fire together more often? More of their shared spikes now include cell 2.

Work out the three-neuron probabilities

With a 50% rate for every cell, exchanging spikes and silences preserves the pair frequencies. Relabeling the three cells also preserves all the observations. The maximum-entropy solution therefore gives 000 and 111 the same probability, a, and each of the six mixed patterns the same probability, b.

All probabilities sum to one, so 2a + 6b = 1. Cells 1 and 3 fire together in 111 or 101, so a + b = 0.30. Substituting a = 0.30 − b into the first equation gives b = 0.10 and a = 0.20.

Where the prediction worked, and where it missed

At exactly ten active neurons, Figure 5B shows about 1.29 bursts per 1,000 windows. The pairwise model predicted 2.15, about 1.7 times too high. The independent prediction had already fallen below 0.001 per 1,000. The paper describes the observed-to-independent ratio as roughly 10,000×. Whether the authors measured 10,000× for the particular 40 neurons shown is unknown. The independent value at ten is off the chart, and the public release does not identify those 40 cells. Figure 5B, page 7

The paper goes one step further. In larger groups, the pairwise model missed rare bursts. The authors added a term depending only on K, so every pattern with the same number of active neurons gets the same adjustment to its log weight. They called this the K-pairwise model. Matching the burst counts is now part of the fit. The telling test came from specific groups of three. In a 100-neuron example, the new model corrected much of the bias in their predicted correlations, even though its new term had no information about which three cells were involved. Figure 7

Try it on the recording

I tested the ten-of-40 comparison on 10,000 randomly chosen, overlapping groups from the same retina. Across groups, the median ratio of observed to predicted burst frequency was 1,463×. 64 groups out of 10,000 reached 10,000×. Which 40 neurons you pick matters.

One group shows why the movie matters, too. Across 99 repeats held out for testing, I counted 57 bursts. Independence using each cell’s average rate predicted 0.048. My separately fitted pairwise model predicted 206. When I let each cell’s firing probability depend on the moment in the movie, independence at each moment predicted 55.9. A passing edge can make several cells more likely to fire at once. Getting the total right still leaves a harder question. Can you predict which ten will fire?
